issues.legal_issue: A landlord cannot rely on an eviction ground that was rejected in the later appellate proceedings and was not pursued after a statutory amendment made that ground unavailable on the evidence.
material_facts: The first appellate court had upheld eviction on the landlord’s personal-requirement ground, but a later statutory amendment changed the applicable requirements.
The single judge held that the evidence did not support eviction on the amended ground, and the landlord did not seek to establish that ground through subsequent events or further evidence.
The landlord did not seriously defend the first appellate court’s finding under the amended provision, and the ground was not canvassed in the further appeal.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was confined to the eviction decree based on rent default; the landlord could not support the decree on the personal-requirement ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 13(1)(ff) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, as amended, the personal-requirement ground had to be assessed under the amended requirements. Because the ground had been rejected in the later appellate proceedings and was not pursued there, it did not remain available to support the decree in this appeal. No earlier cases were relied on for this issue.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The case is an appeal seeking special leave to challenge an eviction decree.
predicates.requirement_ground_rejected_in_later_app: A later appellate court rejected the landlord’s personal-requirement ground under the applicable amended requirements.
predicates.landlord_did_not_pursue_requirement_grou: The landlord did not pursue that ground in the subsequent appellate proceedings.

issues.definition: When a special-leave appeal challenges an eviction decree, a personal-requirement ground rejected in the later appeal and not pursued by the landlord does not remain within the appeal’s scope.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings about whether rent was tendered cannot be reopened in an appeal by special leave merely by seeking a fresh assessment of the evidence.
material_facts: The tenant asserted that the landlord had personally refused rent tendered for a month.
The trial court and first appellate court found that the tenant had not proved the alleged tender and refusal.
The single judge upheld that finding, and the tenant sought to challenge it again in the appeal by special leave.
issues.conclusion: The tenant could not re-agitate the correctness of the concurrent factual finding on personal tender in the appeal by special leave.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution does not permit a party to re-agitate a factual finding based on appreciation of evidence merely by seeking its reappraisal where the finding has been made concurrently by the courts below and approved by the High Court. No earlier cases were relied on for this issue.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The case is an appeal seeking special leave to challenge a judgment.
predicates.concurrent_finding_on_evidence: The courts below made the same factual finding after considering the evidence, and the High Court approved it.
predicates.appellant_seeks_reassessment_of_that_fin: The appellant asks the Supreme Court to reassess the evidence underlying that concurrent finding.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal, a concurrent factual finding based on evidence is not reopened when the appellant merely seeks its reassessment.

issues.legal_issue: Rent remitted after the applicable payment deadline, without proof of an earlier timely tender, does not constitute valid payment that defeats an eviction claim for rent default.
material_facts: The tenant’s personal tender of rent for January was not proved.
The tenant sent rent for January by money order after the statutory deadline for payment of that month’s rent.
After the money order was refused, the tenant deposited the rent with the Rent Controller.
The courts held that the later deposit did not amount to valid payment under the Act.
issues.conclusion: The money order and subsequent deposit did not constitute valid payment of the rent, and the tenant remained in default.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(2) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 required rent to be paid by the fifteenth day of the succeeding month in the absence of a different agreement. In the absence of a proved timely tender, a money order sent after that deadline and a subsequent deposit with the Rent Controller did not constitute valid payment under the Act. No earlier cases were relied on for this issue.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground that a tenant defaulted in paying rent.
predicates.personal_tender_not_proved: The tenant’s alleged timely personal tender of rent was not established.
predicates.money_order_sent_after_rent_deadline: The tenant sent the rent by money order only after the deadline for paying that rent had passed.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding for rent default, rent is not validly paid when the alleged timely personal tender is unproved and the money order is sent after the payment deadline.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant seeking statutory relief from eviction for rent default must make a fresh deposit that complies with the statutory procedure when earlier deposits were invalid.
material_facts: The tenant had deposited rent with the Rent Controller, but those deposits were held invalid under the Act.
The tenant did not withdraw the invalid deposits and make a fresh deposit in accordance with the procedure for obtaining relief from default.
The tenant sought the benefit of the Act’s provision allowing relief from eviction for rent default.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was not entitled to relief from eviction under Section 17(4) because the tenant had not made a fresh deposit in accordance with Section 17(1).
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17(1) and 17(4) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 required a tenant seeking relief from eviction for default to follow the prescribed deposit or payment procedure. The amount to be deposited included rent that the tenant had previously deposited invalidly; Section 22(3) did not make such an invalid deposit payment to the landlord. No earlier cases were relied on for this issue.
